why: Three plain questions plus a closing action for the student's own map; shorter and more concrete.
Keeps the author's first-person story that sets up the payoff; A loses the voice.
Guess prompt comes before the reveal, so the student actually predicts.
Student shapes the rules together with the agent, an active role, rather than the passive-sounding 'not from a blank page'.
Says what to do when the check fails, so the student stays in control.
'One session at a time' is concrete; 'run' is vaguer.
The title states the takeaway the student can picture, and the body is unchanged.
Shorter, and drops the M6 reference the student must recall.
Shorter without losing the point.
The closing line puts the student in control and gives the reason to save it.
'Prompts' is concrete and matches what the student ran; 'exercise' is vaguer.
Names the pushback specifically as the part without a pre-made prompt; clearer.
Shorter, states the practice directly; A's forward reference to Module 4 is abstract orientation the student can't picture yet.
'YOUR real work is the material' is the author's punchy first-person voice; B is flatter.
'The move is the same every time' names the repeatable pattern, which helps the student act on it.
Drops the phase-3/4 preview; fewer words and nothing the student needs now.
Spells out the red-green steps the student is watching, which makes the loop concrete before they read the diff.
'Just a draft' is clearer and reads faster than 'It's a draft' after 'It often isn't'.
Shorter; B's 'you are not learning them here' is a disclaimer that adds noise without helping the student act.
Short, direct instruction to the student, who is the one acting; A's 'watch ... rather than typing along' sets up passive viewing.
'Three' counts a list the student can already see; dropping it is shorter and loses nothing.
'Three pressures' gives the student a concrete count to hold onto, and it matches the three bullets.
'Where the file gets read' says what the slide is about, which is more useful orientation than a bare count.
Shorter and keeps the focus on what the student sees in their own session; B adds an MCP detail that is a distraction here.
Drops the extra 'Three modules in, this is your practice now' line; shorter, and it adds nothing.
Tighter and punchier, and it keeps the first-person voice. It also names the outcomes: the verifier, the sim, ten fixes, and the pushback on 'done'.
Shorter; 'This is your side-quest lane' adds nothing.
Shorter; it drops the 'strong candidate… after you talk to the team' line that hedges and repeats the point.
'Check what Claude proposes' puts the student in control more actively than 'Read'.
The point states a concrete idea the student can picture: recurring work has a shape that is easier to recognise when drawn.
A shorter title that states the benefit and the student's action: a check resets the chain.
An imperative title that tells the student what to do and puts them in control.
It gives the advanced option, asking Claude to set up the built-in status line, and the wording is clearer.
Writing the decision as an ADR is concrete, and the term is spelled out.
Naming 'The wall' gives the student a concept to remember, and it puts the idea in the first person.
The title is a concrete image, a skill outliving the thread, and it is easier to picture than 'compounds'.
'context window' names the concept the body already uses; the extra word carries meaning.
The closing line is honest and in the author's own voice; it sets realistic expectations.
'Five things' tells the reader what to expect and is easy to picture.
The student acts and controls Claude with a concrete ask; 'Spot what's still generic' leaves it unclear who does what.
The closing line stops students from reading the phases as a pipeline, and it's only one short sentence.
'You don't need to get it right first time' is a permission line, which the author values.
Concrete, student-driven and short: take a task, push back twice in your own words.
The orientation lines tell students where they are at a window switch, which the author asks for.
It avoids 'committed' and its git meaning, and 'the change you'd make' puts the student in control.
